summary: Documents the Not-So-Stubby Area option for OSPF. An NSSA is like an OSPF stub area but can still import some external routes in a limited way. It builds on the earlier definition in RFC 1587, with changes that expand capability while staying backward-compatible, so implementations of both interoperate.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF divides a network into areas, and a stub area is one that keeps a short route list instead of the full list. RFC 3101 adds a new kind of area that keeps that short list but can also accept a few routes from another routing protocol and pass them on to the rest of the network.

questions: how do nssa areas import external routes
how does an nssa import external routes
subtitle: An OSPF area that keeps a short route table like a stub area but can still import a few external routes.

tldr.problem: OSPF stub areas keep their route tables small, but by definition they cannot import routes that come from outside the OSPF domain, so a site with its own networks had to run a second routing protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new kind of OSPF area, the not-so-stubby area, in which a new Type-7 link state advertisement carries imported external routes inside the area and an elected border router translates selected Type-7 advertisements into ordinary Type-5 advertisements.
tldr.outcome: Implementations of this memo and of its predecessor RFC 1587 interoperate, because every difference the RFC lists is backward compatible.

facts.label: Default route in an NSSA
facts.value: 0.0.0.0/0, as a Type-3 or Type-7 LSA

today: RFC 3101 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 1587, and the RFC states that implementations of the two interoperate because every difference is backward compatible.

sections.title: Why a Stub Area Is Not Enough
sections.content:
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) splits one routing domain into areas, and a router in a stub area keeps a short list of routes instead of the full list. It reaches destinations outside its own area through a default route. That keeps the link state database small, but it also means the area cannot import routes from outside OSPF.

The RFC describes two situations where that limit hurts. In a transit network, a leaf site may own several IP networks: one is directly connected to a router the transit network runs, and the others are distributed around the site and run with a different protocol such as RIP. The site looks like a single stub entity from outside, but the original OSPF rules make it illegal for that stub area to import the routes learned by RIP. The transit network is forced to run OSPF only to the edge router and to run RIP between the two.

In a corporate network the same problem appears with several non-backbone areas. Those areas want to be stub areas so their routers keep small tables, yet they also want to inject two aggregated external advertisements, one for each of their subnetted address blocks, and to keep a chosen path to each of them through a preferred border router.
sections.plainLanguage: A stub area is a small part of a network that keeps a short list of routes instead of every route in the network. The rules for stub areas also forbid bringing in routes learned from another protocol, which is exactly what some sites need.

sections.title: The Not-So-Stubby Area
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new optional type of OSPF area, humorously called a not-so-stubby area (NSSA), that behaves like a stub area but can import external routes in a limited way. Two things are added to OSPF: an option bit, the N-bit, which makes sure that every router in the area agrees on the area's configuration, and a new link state advertisement, the Type-7 LSA, which carries external route information inside the area.

Type-7 LSAs have almost the same syntax as the Type-5 LSAs that carry external routes in ordinary OSPF areas. Two rules separate them. Type-7 LSAs may be originated inside the NSSA and are flooded only there; as with a stub area, no Type-5 LSA is flooded into the NSSA. And Type-7 LSAs never leave the NSSA on their own, although the information they carry may be passed on afterwards.

To let a limited amount of external information cross the border, an NSSA border router translates selected Type-7 LSAs into Type-5 LSAs and floods those to every area that can carry Type-5 LSAs. Border routers may be configured with address ranges, so that many Type-7 routes collapse into a single Type-5 route. The border routers that do this translation are configurable, and one is elected if none is configured.

Because an NSSA does not receive full routing information, its border router should also originate a default route for the network 0.0.0.0/0 into the area. A Type-7 default LSA originated by a border router is never translated, but one originated by a router inside the NSSA that is not a border router may be.
sections.plainLanguage: The new area type works like a stub area but adds one thing: a way to carry routes that came from outside the network into the area. Those routes stay inside the area until a border router decides to pass them on, and only the ones that are marked for propagation are passed on.

sections.title: The Type-7 LSA
sections.content:
An NSSA AS boundary router, the router that exchanges routing information with another autonomous system, imports external routes into the NSSA as Type-7 LSAs, one for each destination network. Like any OSPF AS boundary router, it says so by setting the E-bit in its router-LSA. The link state database must therefore hold Type-7 LSAs as well.

The RFC lists six points in which a Type-7 LSA differs from a Type-5 LSA. The type field in the LSA header is 7 rather than 5. Type-7 LSAs are flooded only within the NSSA that originated them, following the same rules as Type-1 and Type-2 LSAs. They are listed only in the OSPF area data structures of their own NSSA, so they are area specific, while Type-5 LSAs have global scope. NSSA border routers select which Type-7 LSAs are translated. A Type-7 LSA carries a P-bit that tells a border router to translate it into a Type-5 LSA. And a Type-7 LSA that is to be translated must have its forwarding address set.

The forwarding address is the address to which traffic for the destination is sent. A value of 0.0.0.0 means traffic is sent to the router that originated the LSA. When the next hop of a route learned from the neighbouring autonomous system belongs to a network connected to the NSSA, that next hop is copied into the forwarding address. If the P-bit is set, the forwarding address must not be zero; otherwise it may be. When the interface holding that address goes down, the router picks a new address and re-originates the LSA, or flushes it if there is none.
sections.plainLanguage: A Type-7 advertisement is the message that carries an imported route inside the new kind of area. It looks almost the same as the advertisement OSPF already uses for outside routes, but it carries one extra flag that says whether the route may be passed on, and it names the address that traffic should be sent to.

sections.title: Originating Type-7 LSAs
sections.content:
Only an NSSA AS boundary router may originate Type-7 LSAs into an NSSA. To have a network advertised across the whole OSPF domain, the router must set the P-bit in the LSA header's options field, and the LSA must carry a valid, non-zero forwarding address. If the P-bit is clear, no NSSA border router translates the LSA into a Type-5 LSA.

When one border router originates both a Type-5 LSA and a Type-7 LSA for the same network, the P-bit must be clear in the Type-7 LSA, so that another border router does not translate it a second time. If the border router originates only a Type-7 LSA, it may set the P-bit so the network can be aggregated and propagated during translation.

When two routers in the same NSSA originate equivalent Type-7 LSAs, the router whose LSA is less preferred flushes its copy. Preference is settled by two tie breakers: an LSA with the P-bit set is preferred over one with it clear, and if the P-bit settings match, the LSA with the higher router ID is preferred.

A Type-7 default LSA for the network 0.0.0.0/0 may be originated into the NSSA by any router in it. One originated by a border router must have the P-bit clear, while one originated by an AS boundary router that is not a border router may set it. Border routers may install a Type-7 default LSA only if its P-bit is set. The metric of the default LSA that a border router advertises into its NSSA should be configurable, and for a Type-7 default LSA the metric type, 1 or 2, should be configurable as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Only routers that talk to another network can import routes into the area. Each imported route carries a flag saying whether the area's border router should pass it on to the rest of the network, and a route with that flag set must also name a real next-hop address.

sections.title: Calculating Type-7 External Routes
sections.content:
The RFC rewrites the part of OSPF that calculates external routes so that it can handle Type-7 LSAs as well as Type-5 LSAs. Each AS-external LSA is examined in turn. An LSA whose metric is LSInfinity, or whose age is MaxAge, is skipped, and so is one the calculating router originated itself.

The destination is the LSA's link state ID masked with the network mask from the LSA body. The router then looks up the entry for the AS boundary router that originated the LSA. For a Type-5 LSA the entry must come from an attached area that can carry Type-5 LSAs; for a Type-7 LSA the entry must come from the NSSA that originated it, because a Type-7 LSA does not travel any further. If no such entry exists, the LSA is ignored.

A Type-7 default LSA is ignored when the calculating router is a border router and either the LSA has its P-bit clear, or the router is suppressing the import of summary routes. Otherwise the LSA describes a path to an external destination. If the forwarding address is 0.0.0.0, packets go to the originating router, and for a Type-7 LSA the routing entry must be taken from the originating NSSA. If the forwarding address is not zero, it must resolve to an intra-area path inside the same NSSA. Only then is the path computed: the cost of the internal path to the originating router or forwarding address is added to the external metric for a type 1 external route, while a type 2 external route keeps the internal cost separate from the advertised type 2 metric.

Internal paths always win over external ones, and type 1 external paths win over type 2 external paths. When two LSA instances describe the same destination, cost and forwarding address, a Type-7 LSA with the P-bit set is preferred, then a Type-5 LSA, then the LSA with the higher router ID.

The RFC warns of a catch in Appendix E. A non-default Type-7 LSA with the P-bit clear may still be installed in the routing table of a border router, and because such a route is never propagated, traffic that passes through that border router can be pulled into the NSSA against the sender's intent. The same happens for routes covered by an address range configured with DoNotAdvertise.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that receives an imported route uses it only when it can reach the router that sent the route, and only through the area the route came from. Routes learned inside the network always beat routes learned outside it.

sections.title: Electing the Translator
sections.content:
Every NSSA border router is a potential translator, but running several of them is not recommended unless packets have to be routed efficiently through the backbone to an NSSA that has been split by Type-7 address ranges. Too many translators needlessly enlarge the link state database.

Two area parameters control this. NSSATranslatorRole says whether a border router always translates or takes part in an election; the values are Always and Candidate, and the default is Candidate. NSSATranslatorState is kept in the area data structure and starts as disabled; it becomes enabled or elected, and back to disabled when the router is no longer a border router.

A new bit, Nt, appears in the router-LSAs of NSSAs. Routers clear it by default, but a border router with its translator state enabled sets it. A border router whose role is Always re-originates its router-LSA whenever that state changes.

A candidate border router keeps a list of the border routers that it can reach both over the NSSA and, as AS boundary routers, over the transit topology. If any router on that list has its Nt bit set or has a higher router ID, the candidate disables itself. Otherwise its state becomes elected. An elected translator keeps translating until it is superseded by a reachable border router with the Nt bit set or a higher router ID, which can happen when a router with role Always regains border status or when a partitioned NSSA becomes whole again. A translator that decides its services are no longer needed keeps translating for the TranslatorStabilityInterval, whose default value is 40 seconds, which limits the flushing of translated LSAs.

All NSSA border routers must set the E-bit in the Type-1 router-LSAs they originate into directly attached areas that are not stub areas, even when they are not translating. Otherwise other border routers cannot see their status and the election may pick unnecessary translators.
sections.plainLanguage: When an area has several border routers, only one of them normally turns the imported routes into ordinary outside routes, so that the network does not carry the same information many times over. If no router is set to do this job on purpose, the routers agree on one by a simple rule, and the new router keeps the job for a short while after being replaced so that the network does not churn.

sections.title: Translating and Aggregating Type-7 LSAs
sections.content:
The translation runs as part of the NSSA's Dijkstra calculation, after the Type-5 and Type-7 routes have been calculated, and only on a router that is currently an NSSA translator. Locally originated Type-7 LSAs are processed first, because a Type-5 LSA produced by translation can displace one that a local OSPF external source produced, and re-origination of the local one is then held back until the translated LSA is flushed.

A Type-7 LSA is translatable when its P-bit is set, its forwarding address is not 0.0.0.0, and the most specific Type-7 address range that covers its network does not have DoNotAdvertise status. A translatable LSA that is not covered by any configured address range produces a Type-5 LSA with the same network, mask, path type, metric, forwarding address and external route tag. Its advertising router field is the router ID of the border router, and its link state ID is the network address.

When the LSA is covered by a configured address range, the range aggregates it. The path type and metric of the range come from the translatable LSAs that best match it: if any of them has path type 2, the range has path type 2, otherwise path type 1. A path type 1 range takes the highest cost among those LSAs; a path type 2 range takes the highest type 2 cost plus one, so the aggregate never looks closer to the border than the route it covers. The aggregated Type-5 LSA takes the range's network mask and external route tag, and its forwarding address is set to 0.0.0.0. At most one Type-5 LSA is originated for each address range.

The RFC works through an example. A range of [10.0.0.0, 255.0.0.0] that covers 10.1.0.0/24 with path type 1 and cost 10, 10.2.0.0/24 with path type 1 and cost 11, and 10.3.0.0/24 with path type 2 and type 2 cost 5 produces a Type-5 LSA with path type 2 and metric 6. If the third route also has path type 1 and cost 5, the same range produces a Type-5 LSA with path type 1 and metric 11. These rules avoid routing loops when both path types are used inside the area.

When a translated or aggregated Type-5 LSA should no longer exist, the border router flushes it or re-originates it from other Type-7 LSAs. A border router that has been deposed keeps its translated Type-5 LSAs until they age out normally, but flushes the ones it produced by aggregation once the TranslatorStabilityInterval has passed, so that the new translator's path is not short-circuited.
sections.plainLanguage: When a border router passes routes on, it can also group them: many imported routes that fall inside one address range become a single outside route. The cost of the group is set so that it never looks like a shorter path than the routes it replaces, which keeps traffic from looping.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats two kinds of threat to a routing protocol: authenticating the routing information, and denial of service through floods of advertisements. It notes that both concerns exist whether or not a router supports the NSSA option.

OSPF authenticates its own protocol exchanges, and the type of authentication can be configured per network segment. The cryptographic authentication option is believed to be secure against passive attacks and to give significant protection against active attacks: each router appends a message digest to the packets it sends, and receivers check the digest with the shared secret key. The protection depends on the strength of the digest algorithm, MD5 being the only one specified at the time, on the strength of the key, and on every implementation being correct. All parties must also keep the shared secret secret. None of the standard OSPF authentication types provide confidentiality, and none protect against traffic analysis.

For floods, OSPF limits how often a new instance of any LSA may be originated, once every MinLSInterval seconds, whose value is 5 seconds, and how often a new instance may be accepted during flooding, once every MinLSArrival seconds, whose value is 1 second.

Proper operation of OSPF requires every router to keep an identical copy of the link state database. When the database grows too large for a router with limited resources, which the RFC calls database overflow, routers with small resources can be accommodated by configuring stub areas and NSSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says the same warnings apply here as elsewhere in OSPF. The protocol can be authenticated so that a receiver knows the advertisement came from a real neighbour, but the authentication does not hide the routing information. OSPF also limits how often a router may repeat an advertisement, so that one router cannot flood the network by repeating itself.
